title: Transformers as Measure-Theoretic Associative Memory: A Statistical Perspective and Minimax Optimality
claim: Associative recall decomposes into two stages: select the relevant component from a mixture given a query, then predict from it.
layout: 3 boxes, left-to-right, labeled arrows 'recall' and 'predict', dashed vs solid components
description: Three rounded rectangles are arranged left to right and joined by two arrows labeled 'recall' and 'predict'. Each box has three small boxes at the top, which stand for component measures μ^(1), μ^(2) and μ^(3). The left box is titled 'Mixture ∝ Σ μ^(i); + Query x_q(i*)' and shows all three components as solid boxes. The middle box is titled 'Select index i*' and shows a mapping from the averaged mixture to μ^(i*). In it, components 1 and 2 are dashed and faded, and component 3 has a thick solid border to mark it as selected. The right box is titled 'Evaluate F̃*(μ_0^(i*); , x_q)' and keeps the same dashed and thick-border highlighting. The eye goes first to the thick-bordered selected component, then follows the arrows. The figure is black and white and relies on math notation.
caption: Associative recall at the level of measures (informal): the query xq(i∗) selects the relevant component measure µ(i∗)
abstract: Transformers excel through content-addressable retrieval and the ability to exploit contexts of, in principle, unbounded length. We recast associative memory at the level of probability measures, treating a context as a distribution over tokens and viewing attention as an integral operator on measures. Concretely, for mixture contexts $Î½= I^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^I Î¼^{(i^*)}$ and a query $x_{\mathrm{q}}(i^*)$, the task decomposes into (i) recall of the relevant component $Î¼^{(i^*)}$ and (ii) prediction from $(Î¼_{i^*},x_\mathrm{q})$. We study learned softmax attention (not a frozen kernel) trained by empirical risk minimization and show that a shallow measure-theoretic Transformer composed with an MLP learns the recall-and-predict map under a spectral assumption on the input densities. We further establish a matching minimax lower bound with the same rate exponent (up to multiplicative constants), proving sharpness of the convergence order. The framework offers a principled recipe for designing and analyzing Transformers that recall from arbitrarily long, distributional contexts with provable generalization guarantees.
